items.title: Roswell Rudd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998
items.q: Albert Ayler on the tenor and soprano saxophones with Cecil Taylor on the piano, Sunny Murray on the drums and Louis Worrell on the bass, playing together in a coffee house in Greenwich Village in 1961 or something.

ctx.x: That’s not playing would set up something to play next, or as an answer to something you had played, to put a space there.

Yeah. The call-response is the thing that I teach right at the beginning. And the idea with this is that it’s better to wait if an idea doesn’t come right away. And then you have the advantage of being with one, two, three, four other, five other people. And this is a great chance for some kind of dialogue to happen. And this to me is basic in the music. If I don’t hear the call and response and the music never has a chance to breathe, it eliminates one of the great ways that I have of getting into it. If I hear…
with each other. I mean they were just like firing off guns and stuff, musically, with each other.
